This hymn is generally thought to be one of the most loved hymns written during the latter part of the 19th century. The writing of this thoughtful and beautifully constructed text is even more amazing when we consider that its author was one who was almost completely blind and who describes the writing of this hymn as the “fruit of much mental suffering,” and “the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life.”

Born in Glasgow, Scotland, March 27, 1842, George Matheson had only partial vision as a boy, and, after entering Glasgow University, his eyesight continued to fail rapidly. Except for “moments of shadowy eyesight”, he was totally blind by the age of 18. This affliction of blindness seemed to be a tragedy since he was an eager and avid scholar, yet it caused him to trust in the Lord, and it strengthened his walk with God.

He entered the university at the early age of 15 and graduated with high honors in 1861 at the age of 19. He was a brilliant scholar, even spending four more years after graduation in more theological studies, all the while remaining single. After his graduation he became entirely dependent on others, relying much upon his two sisters, who were so dedicated that they learned Latin, Greek, and Hebrew since they thought it might aid him in his theological studies. One of them continued to be his faithful co-worker and helper throughout his life, assisting in his calling of being a pastor and other ministerial duties.

After completing his theological course, he became assistant pastor to the renowned Dr. Macduff, in whose church of thousands of members he had been brought up. Soon, however, he was chosen minister of the Church of Scotland in the seaport summer resort of Innellan. Here he stayed for eighteen years. Many families came to spend the summer there chiefly to be inspired by his preaching ministry.

Whenever he preached, the open Bible was before him as he stood in the pulpit, and to the congregation, he seemed to be reading from it. During the messages, his eyes looked straight at the congregation, and many went away with no clue that they just listened to a blind preacher. It was during this time that he made a practice of memorizing his sermons, as well as the passages of Scripture he used in his messages. His memory was so sharp that if someone read one of his prepared sermons to him twice, or whatever else he wanted to memorize, he could from then on repeat it perfectly. One Sunday, however, after doing this for 12 years, when in the middle of a powerful sermon his memory completely collapsed, and the topic on which he was preaching vanished from his mind. He sat down and commenced to request a psalm to be sung, and, after the song, with perfect calmness told the audience what had happened. With this done, he stood to his feet, gave out a new text, and preached an impromptu sermon of great power. After that experience George wrote little of his sermons, and finally prepared only an outline from which to preach.

Dr. Matheson’s final pastorate was taken up in 1886 at the age of 44 where he became pastor of the large St. Bernard’s Parish Church in Edinburgh, where his eloquent preaching consistently attracted large throngs of people to the services. Here he remained for 13 years, his church growing from 1,494 members to 1,703 in the first 5 years. He continued faithfully preaching the gospel and became well known as one of Scotland’s outstanding preachers and pastors and was greatly esteemed in Edinburgh where he resided.

Many speculations have been made regarding the cause of the mental distress which prompted the author to write this text. A very popular account, although never verified, is that this text was a result of the severe trial Matheson faced after his soon-to-be bride left him just before their marriage when she learned of his impending total blindness. Although this story cannot be documented, there are many significant hints in this hymn reflecting a saddened heart, such as the “flickering torch” and the “borrowed ray” in the second verse, the tracing of the “rainbow through the rain” in the third stanza, as well as the “cross” in the last verse.

Fortunately, Dr. Matheson did relate an account of his writing of this hymn:

“My hymn was composed in the manse of Innellan on the evening of June 6, 1882. I was at that time alone. It was the day of my sister’s wedding, and the rest of the family were staying overnight in Glasgow. Something happened to me, which was known only to myself, and which caused me the most severe mental suffering. The hymn was the fruit of that suffering and was the quickest bit of work I ever did in my life. A genuine inspiration, I had the impression rather of having it dictated to me by some inward voice than of working it out myself. I am quite sure that the whole work was completed in five minutes and equally sure it never received at my hands any retouching or correction. I have no natural gift of rhythm. All the other verses I have ever written are manufactured articles; this came like a dayspring from on high. I have never been able to gain once more the same fervor in verse.”

The hymn first appeared in the Church of Scotland monthly magazine, Life and Work, in January 1883. The tune was composed one year later by a prominent Scotch organist of his day, Albert L. Peace, who was asked to write a tune especially for Matheson’s text.

Peace’s own account of the writing of this fine tune is as follows, “After reading it over carefully, I wrote the music straight off, and may say that the ink of the first note was hardly dry when I had finished the tune.” The origin or the tune name, St. Margaret, is unknown except that it is a name much revered in Scotland, and certainly because of the beloved Queen Margaret of Scotland.

The later years of Matheson’s life from the age of 57 to his death at age 64 were spent in writing some of the finest devotional writings in the English tongue, including Moments on the Mount, Voice of the Spirit, and Rests by the River. Although this is his only hymn found in most hymnals, he did write a few other fine hymns, including “Make Me A Captive Lord”, and “Then I Shall Be Free.”

The four key words of “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” are: love, light, joy, and cross. These words have been described as the complete satisfaction for any believer whose life is totally surrendered to the will of God. It could take the rest of one’s life to completely discover the personal significance of these four expressions.

Hierdie gesang word algemeen beskou as een van die mees geliefde gesange wat geskryf is gedurende die laaste deel van die 19de eeu. Die skryf van hierdie bedagsame en beeldskoon opgeboude teks is nog meer verstommend as ons in ag neem dat die skrywer byna heeltemal blind was en die skryf van hierdie gesang beskryf as die “vrug van baie geestelike lyding,” en “die vinnigste stukkie werk wat ek ooit in my lewe gedoen het.”

Gebore in Glasgow, Skotland, op 27 Maart 1842, het George Matheson as seun net gedeeltelike sig gehad, en nadat hy aan die Universiteit van Glasgow begin het, het sy sig vinnig aangehou agteruitgaan. Behalwe vir “oomblikke van skemeragtige sig,” was hy teen die ouderdom van 18 totaal blind. Hierdie belangrike beproewing van blindheid het na alle voorkoms ’n tragedie gelyk aangesien hy ’n ywerige en gretige geleerde was, maar dit het hom daartoe gelei om op die Here te vertrou, en dit het sy wandel met God versterk.

Hy het op die vroeë ouderdom van 15 in die universiteit begin en het in 1861 op 19-jarige ouderdom met hoë lof geëindig. Hy was ’n briljante geleerde en het selfs vier verdere jare ná die gradeplegtigheid in meer teologiese studies deurgebring, terwyl hy ongetroud gebly het. Na sy gradeplegtigheid het hy heeltemal afhanklik van ander geword, en baie op sy twee susters staatgemaak, wat so toegewy was dat hulle Latyn, Grieks en Hebreeus geleer het omdat hulle gedink het dit sou hom in sy teologiese studies kon help. Een van hulle het sy getroue mede-werker en helper deur sy lewe gebly en hom ondersteun in sy roeping as predikant en ander ampspligte.

Na voltooiing van sy teologiese kursus het hy assistentpredikant geword by die beroemde Dr. Macduff, in wie se kerk met duisende lede hy grootgemaak is. Binne kort is hy egter gekies as predikant van die Church of Scotland in die hawedorp en somerresort Innellan. Hier het hy agtien jaar gebly. Baie families het die somer daar deurgebring hoofsaaklik om deur sy prediking geïnspireer te word.

Wanneer hy gepreek het, het die oop Bybel voor hom op die kansel geleë gestaan, en vir die gemeente het dit gelyk asof hy daaruit lees. Gedurende die toesprake het sy oë reguit na die gemeente gekyk, en baie het weggegaan sonder ’n idee dat hulle net na ’n blinde prediker geluister het. Dit was gedurende hierdie tyd dat hy die gewoonte ontwikkel het om sy preke uit die hoof te leer, sowel as die Skrifafdelings wat hy in sy toesprake gebruik het. Sy geheue was so skerp dat as iemand een van sy voorbereide preke twee keer vir hom gelees het, of wat ook al hy wou memoriseer, hy dit van daardie punt af perfek kon herhaal. Op een Sondag egter, nadat hy dit vir 12 jaar so gedoen het, het sy geheue heeltemal in die middel van ’n kragtige preek ineenstort en het die onderwerp waarop hy gepreek het uit sy gedagtes verdwyn. Hy het gaan sit en ’n psalm aangevra om gesing te word, en ná die lied, met volmaakte kalmte aan die gehoor vertel wat gebeur het. Nadat dit gedoen was, het hy opgestaan, ’n nuwe teks uitgedeel en ’n geïmproviseerde preek van groot krag gelewer. Na daardie ervaring het George min van sy preke geskryf, en uiteindelik slegs ’n oorsig voorberei waarvan hy gepreek het.

Dr. Matheson se laaste amp as predikant het hy in 1886 op 44-jarige ouderdom aangeneem toe hy predikant geword het van die groot St. Bernard’s Parish Church in Edinburgh, waar sy welsprekende prediking konsekwent groot skares mense na die eredienste gelok het. Hier het hy 13 jaar gebly en sy kerk het van 1 494 lede tot 1 703 in die eerste vyf jaar gegroei. Hy het getrou die evangelie gebly predikend en het bekend geword as een van Skotland se uitstaande predikers en predikante en is hoog geag in Edinburgh waar hy gewoon het.

Daar is baie spekulasies gemaak oor die oorsaak van die geestelike nood wat die outeur aangespoor het om hierdie teks te skryf. ’n Baie gewilde verhaal, alhoewel nooit bevestig nie, is dat hierdie teks die gevolg was van die ernstige beproewing wat Matheson moes deurmaak nadat sy tulebruid hom net voor hul troue verlaat het toe sy van sy naderende totale blindheid verneem het. Al kan hierdie verhaal nie gedokumenteer word nie, is daar baie betekenisvolle aanduidings in hierdie gesang wat ’n bedroefde hart weerspieël, soos die “flikkerende toorts” en die “geleende straal” in die tweede vers, die nasporing van die “reënboog deur die reën” in die derde refrein, sowel as die “kruis” in die laaste vers.

Gelukkig het Dr. Matheson wel ’n rekening gegee van die skryf van hierdie gesang:

“My gesang is gecomponeer in die predikantswoning van Innellan op die aand van 6 Junie 1882. Ek was daardie tyd alleen. Dit was die dag van my suster se huwelik, en die res van die familie het oornag in Glasgow gebly. Iets het met my gebeur wat net vir myself bekend was, en wat my die ergste geestelike lyding veroorsaak het. Die gesang was die vrug van daardie lyding en was die vinnigste stukkie werk wat ek ooit in my lewe gedoen het. ’n Ware inspirasie — ek het eerder die indruk gehad dat dit vir my van ’n innerlike stem af gedikteer is as dat ek dit self uitgedink het. Ek is heel seker dat die hele werk in vyf minute voltooi is en ewe seker dat dit nooit deur my hande geretoucheer of gekorrigeer is nie. Ek het geen natuurlike gawe vir ritme nie. Al die ander verse wat ek ooit geskryf het is vervaardigde artikels; dit het soos ’n dagbreek van bo gekom. Ek het nooit weer daarin geslaag om dieselfde ywer in vers te herwin nie.”

Die gesang het eerste in die Church of Scotland se maandelikse tydskrif, Lewe en Werk, in Januarie 1883 verskyn. Die melodie is een jaar later deur ’n prominente Skotse orrelis van sy tyd, Albert L. Peace, gecomponeer, wat versoek is om ’n musiekstuk spesiaal vir Matheson se teks te skryf.

Peace se eie beskrywing van die skryf van hierdie fyn melodie is soos volg: “Ná dit sorgvuldig deur te lees, het ek die musiek reguit neergeskryf, en ek kan sê dat die ink van die eerste noot skaars droog was toe ek die melodie klaar gehad het.” Die oorsprong van of die naam van die melodie, St. Margaret, is onbekend behalwe dat dit ’n naam is wat in Skotland baie vereer word, en sekerlik ook vanweë die geliefde Koningin Margaret van Skotland.

Die later jare van Matheson se lewe van die ouderdom van 57 tot sy dood op 64 is bestee aan die skryf van sommige van die mooiste vroom skrifte in die Engelse taal, insluitend Moomente op die Berg, Stem van die Gees, en Rus by die Rivier. Alhoewel dit sy enigste gesang is wat in die meeste liedereboeke gevind word, het hy ’n paar ander uitstekende gesange geskryf, insluitende “Make Me A Captive Lord”, en “Then I Shall Be Free.”

Die vier sleutelwoorde van “O Love, That Wilt Not Let Me Go” is: liefde, lig, vreugde, en kruis. Hierdie woorde is beskryf as die volledige voldoening vir enige gelowige wie se lewe totaal oorgegee is aan die wil van God. Dit sou die res van iemand se lewe kan neem om die persoonlike betekenis van hierdie vier uitdrukkings ten volle te ontdek.

Composer       -Albert L. Peace, 1844 – 1912

It was the proverbial “perfect world” that Adam and Eve enjoyed daily with their Creator. The beautiful garden, designed, created, and hand-planted by God Himself, was perfect in every way. We all know that it didn’t stay like that for very long. Because of the privilege of choice that God gave to all mankind, they both soon made the wrong choice. Eve, although deceived by Satan in the form of the serpent, believed the lie and chose to disobey God, doing the only thing that God had lovingly asked her not to do. But when she brought the fruit to Adam, he wasn’t deceived. He knew it was wrong. God was not surprised but, nevertheless, was very disappointed. In Genesis 3, we read the sad account of mankind being expelled from the garden, barred from the tree of eternal life, and the curse being pronounced because of Adam and Eve’s sin. It seemed so dark and hopeless. Even though it was only one man who sinned, the curse passed on to all of the created world, including the earth, plants, and animals. Just consider with me what all came along with this mighty curse.

  1. Disease
  2. Distress and Pain
  3. Deterioration and destruction
  4. Dominance of certain plants like thorns and thistles
  5. Death
  6. Decomposition and Decay

We’ll refer to them today as the six “D’s” of the curse.

Disease

The world’s pristine days of eternal, perfect health were past. Disease entered the picture as part of the curse of sin. The children of men, the birds, beasts, and the plants would all begin to experience the effects of sickness and disease. But God was faithful by providing instructions that helped man to know how to avoid many preventable sicknesses by cleanliness and simple obedience. For example, God’s command to honor His original intent in marriage, maintain purity, avoid multiple potential diseases, etc. He was also interested in our spiritual condition. God never designed mankind to bear guilt. He wants us to have and keep our conscience clear because He knows that a guilty conscience can make you sick!

Some of these sicknesses would be unavoidable, but many could be prevented by building immunity. God was also faithful in designing people, plants, and animals with a regenerative microbiome (billions of helpful bacteria) and a systemic immune system, which helps us fight off diseases. It is amazing how each plant seems to have certain dietary or healing properties that are beneficial. How faithful a Creator!

Distress and Pain

I suspect there was no real reason for any pain in the Garden of Eden, but we have experienced pain ever since the day of their exit. Pain is indeed a part of many of our lives. There are many types of pain. Grief, sorrow, and rejection are all emotional pains that come with the curse. Aches, migraines, sore muscles, torn ligaments, infected tendons, worn joints, and broken bones are a few of the physical pains that we may experience sometime before our last breath. Again, God has been faithful in helping mankind understand what to do to relieve some of life’s pains and distresses. From ancient times, plants, herbs, and other remedies have helped people deal with pain and distress. To this day, we have many useful plants that help us with pain.

One of the most beautiful things that can be experienced on earth is the birth of a child. Yet birth is generally accompanied by much pain. Although we can’t eliminate this promised pain, God has been faithful in providing and revealing to us the use of many herbs for use before, during, and after birth to ease the pain and hasten recovery. He didn’t have to do that for us. Mankind really deserves no mercy. What a faithful Creator!

Deterioration and destruction

We don’t need to study history much to see this principle at work. Wind, rain, and sun all have deteriorating effects on many things. Whether we consider an eroded stream bank, the rocks worn smooth in the riverbed, or the tree blown over by the wind, these are all natural elements of destruction. But add to that what man has done to the plants, animals, the soil, and each other. Whether the devastating effects of destruction during the awful wars or self-centered and greedy practices during peace, man is a very destructive creature. God granted mankind dominion over all of creation. However, too often, we falsely interpret that to mean that we own this sphere called earth and can do whatever we want to with it. He who declared, “The earth is the Lord’s,” doesn’t agree with the idea that men are something other than stewards of God’s creation. It is indeed wicked to worship the created world or anything in it. But it is equally wicked to be unthankful and careless with our Creator’s creation! Nevertheless, God has faithfully designed His earth with regenerative capabilities in the midst of this curse. Bless our gracious Maker!

Dominance of Thorns and Thistles

Anyone who has ever gardened soon found the reality of the battle with weeds. In all fairness, any plant growing where it isn’t desired is a “weed.” Many weeds can be very beneficial plants if we only know what to use them for. Some of the plants that we call weeds are actually quite nutritious and healthy once we understand which ones are edible and how to prepare them. Today, we want to think about thorns and thistles. We need to assume they were created on the first six days, not after the curse was pronounced. It seems that their ability to outgrow the useful crops increased after the curse. Even in this part of the curse, we see God mercifully providing for us.

We grow the artichoke for its bitter leaves, which are used to make digestive bitters. Think about it: Blessed Thistle, Milk Thistle, Teasel, Raspberry Leaf, and Blackberry roots are only a few examples of members of these “thorny weeds” used for medicinal and other food benefits. How good of God to give us benefits in the middle of the very curse!

Death

This is the one “D” that most of us would rather not talk about. In reality, when we take our first breath, we are one breath closer to death. Although all plants, animals, and people will eventually die, we still don’t feel comfortable with it. It is quite normal for us to have a will to live, and if we don’t, we should seek some help to find out why.

Indeed, death has no age. In my lifetime, I have helped bury stillborn babies, people as old as 96 years old, and every age in between. We read of the beautiful paradise restored, seen by the Apostle John in Revelation, as he describes Heaven. Some of the things he mentions are no sickness, no sorrow, no separation, no tears, no more suffering, and no death. In a way, life is only a gestation period for eternity. We can’t stay here, just like the baby in the womb can’t decide that it doesn’t want to enter the real world. With all our sorrows and temptations, our bodies wear out and decay. With all the violence, sin, and wickedness around us, would we really want to stay here in this condition forever? Rather, we return to the soil that we were made from, ashes to ashes and dust to dust, awaiting the final resurrection. Wasn’t it gracious of our faithful God not to allow sinful man to eat of the tree of life in his current sinful, dying state? Can we see and be grateful for God’s faithfulness in providing physical death?

In the midst of the curse given to Eve, the first prophecy of the Messiah is revealed. “And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel” (Genesis 3:15). He is the conqueror of death! Praise God for His Faithfulness.

Decomposition and Decay

Decomposition and Decay are another “D” of the curse. A nut falls to the ground, and a sprout soon appears. In a few years, it will be a small sapling. Years go by, and squirrels gather the acorns that fall to the ground each autumn. Then as a mighty oak it contracts a virus, dies, and in a few years is brought to the ground by a windstorm. Here, it returns to the soil as it decays and decomposes. Ever since the curse, everything rots and decays. Considering all the plants, animals, and people that have died in the last 6,000 years, isn’t it good of God to have designed decomposition and decay? What would this world look like if all the debris of 6,000 years were still lying around? The earth would be covered with dead trees and corpses! This may be hard to realize, but God designed entire kingdoms in creation just to accomplish this before it was even needed because He foresaw the need. The kingdoms of yeast, mold, and fungus, the kingdoms of bacteria, enzymes, and microscopic plant and animal life all help break down the fiber of life and make it into the perfect fertilizer for the completion of the life cycle and provision for the next generation. Healthy organic soil has about 8 billion soil microbes in a single tablespoon. This is another reason why it is so important to treat the soil with respect, not harsh chemicals.

Have you ever considered the great flood of Noah? Imagine the millions of tons of plant, animal, and human matter floating around before finally settling to the bottom and quickly being buried in sediment as the waters receded. This produced the ideal conditions to make coal and the other fossil fuels that we use today. There it was, deep within the earth, until the day it was discovered. To this day, it is still being used.

May we be responsible and faithful stewards of the Lord’s earth!

“For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God. For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who subjected the same in hope. Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now. And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the first fruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:19-23).

Dit was die spreekwoordelike “perfekte wêreld” wat Adam en Eva daagliks saam met hul Skepper geniet het. Die pragtige tuin, ontwerp, geskep en met die hand geplant deur God self, was in elke opsig volmaak. Ons weet almal dat dit nie vir lank so gebly het nie. As gevolg van die keusevoorreg wat God aan die mensdom gegee het, het hulle albei gou die verkeerde keuse gemaak. Eva, alhoewel deur Satan in die gedaante van die slang mislei, het die leuen geglo en gekies om God te ongehoorsaam — die enigste ding wat God liefdevol aan haar gevra het om nie te doen nie. Maar toe sy die vrug aan Adam bring, was hy nie mislei nie. Hy het geweet dit was verkeerd. God was nie verras nie, maar tog baie teleurgesteld. In Genesis 3 lees ons die hartseer verslag van die mensdom wat uit die tuin verdryf is, van die boom van die ewige lewe uitgesluit is en die vloek uitgespreek is as gevolg van Adam en Eva se sonde. Dit het so donker en hopeloos gelyk. Alhoewel dit net een man was wat gesondig het, het die vloek na die hele geskape wêreld oorgedra, insluitend die aarde, plante en diere. Dink saam met my oor wat alles saam met hierdie magtige vloek gekom het.

  1. Siekte
  2. Angs en Pyn
  3. Aftakeling en vernietiging
  4. Oordomsyn van sekere plante soos dorings en distels
  5. Dood
  6. Ontbinding en bederf

Ons sal hulle vandag na verwys as die ses “D’e” van die vloek.

Siekte

Die wêreld se ongerepte dae van ewige, volmaakte gesondheid was verby. Siekte het as deel van die sondevloek in die prentjie gekom. Die kinders van die mense, die voëls, die diere en die plante sou almal die gevolge van siekte en ongesteldheid begin ervaar. Maar God was getrou deur instruksies te verskaf wat die mens help om te weet hoe om baie voorkombare siektes deur netheid en eenvoudige gehoorsaamheid te vermy. Byvoorbeeld, God se opdrag om sy oorspronklike bedoeling in die huwelik te eer, reinheid te handhaaf, verskeie moontlike siektes te vermy, ensovoorts. Hy was ook in ons geestelike toestand belangstelend. God het die mensdom nooit ontwerp om skuld te dra nie. Hy wil hê ons moet ons gewete skoon hê omdat Hy weet dat ’n skuldig gewete jou siek kan maak!

Sommige van hierdie siektes sou onvermydelik wees, maar baie kon verhoed word deur immuniteit op te bou. God was ook getrou om mense, plante en diere te ontwerp met ’n regeneratiewe mikrobiome (miljarde nuttige bakterieë) en ’n sistemiese immuunstelsel, wat ons help om siektes af te weer. Dit is verbasend hoe elke plant blykbaar sekere dieet- of genesingseienskappe het wat voordelig is. Hoe getrou is ons Skepper nie!

Angs en Pyn

Ek vermoed daar was geen regte rede vir pyn in die Tuin van Eden nie, maar ons het pyn ervaar sedert die dag van hul uittog. Pyn is inderdaad deel van baie van ons lewens. Daar is baie tipes pyn. Rou, bedroefheid en afwysing is almal emosionele pyn wat met die vloek kom. Pyn, migraine, seer spiere, geskeurde ligament, geïnfekteerde senings, verslete gewrigte en gebreekte bene is ’n paar van die fisiese pyn wat ons eendag voor ons laaste asem kan ervaar. Weereens het God getrou behulp gespring om die mensdom te laat verstaan wat om te doen om sommige van die pyn en angs van die lewe te verlig. Van antieke tye af het plante, kruie en ander middels mense gehelp om met pyn en angs te handel. Tot vandag toe het ons baie nuttige plante wat ons met pyn help.

Een van die mooiste dinge wat op aarde ervaar kan word, is die geboorte van ’n kind. Tog gaan geboorte gewoonlik gepaard met baie pyn. Alhoewel ons hierdie beloofde pyn nie kan uitskakel nie, was God getrou om vir ons die gebruik van baie kruie voor, tydens en na geboorte te voorsien en onthul om die pyn te verlig en die herstel te bespoedig. Hy moes dit nie vir ons doen nie. Die mensdom verdien regtig geen barmhartigheid nie. Wat ’n getroue Skepper!

Aftakeling en vernietiging

Ons hoef nie baie geskiedenis te bestudeer om hierdie beginsel in werking te sien nie. Wind, reën en son het almal aftakelende effekte op baie dinge. Of ons nou ’n geërodeerde stroomoewer, die rotse wat gladgeslyp is in die rivierbed, of die boom wat deur die wind omgewaai is oorweeg, dit is alles natuurlike elemente van vernietiging. Maar voeg daartoe wat die mens aan die plante, diere, die grond en mekaar gedoen het. Of dit nou die verwoestende gevolge van vernietiging tydens die afgryslike oorloge is of selfsugtige en gierige praktyke gedurende vrede — die mens is ’n baie vernietigende skepsel. God het die mens oor alle skepping heerskappy gegee. Te dikwels interpreteer ons dit egter verkeerdlik asof ons hierdie sfeer wat aarde genoem word besit en daarmee mag doen wat ons wil. Hy wat verklaar het: “Die aarde behoort aan die Here,” stem nie saam met die idee dat mense iets anders as bestuurders van God se skepping is nie. Dit is inderdaad goddeloos om die geskape wêreld of enigiets daarin te aanbid. Maar dit is ewe goddeloos om ondankbaar en onverskillig met ons Skepper se skepping te wees! Nietemin het God getrou sy aarde met regenererende vermoëns ontwerp te midde van hierdie vloek. Geseënd sy genadige Maker!

Oordomsyn van dorings en distels

Enigeen wat al tuingemaak het, het gou die werklikheid van die stryd met onkruid ervaar. In alle regverdigheid is enige plant wat groei waar dit nie gewen word nie, ’n “onkruid.” Baie onkruide kan baie nuttige plante wees as ons net weet waarvoor om hulle te gebruik. Sommige van die plante wat ons onkruid noem, is eintlik baie voedsaam en gesond sodra ons verstaan watter een eetbaar is en hoe om dit voor te berei. Vandag wil ons dink oor dorings en distels. Ons moet aanvaar dat hulle in die eerste ses dae geskep is, nie nádat die vloek uitgespreek is nie. Dit lyk asof hul vermoë om die nuttige gewasse te oorgroei ná die vloek toegeneem het. Selfs in hierdie deel van die vloek sien ons God barmhartig vir ons voorsien.

Ons kweek die artisjok vir sy bitter blare, wat gebruik word om spysverteringsbittere te maak. Dink daaraan: Blessed Thistle (gesegnde distel), Milk Thistle (melkdistel), Teasel (kardeboom), framboosblare en swartbessiewortels is net ’n paar voorbeelde van lede van hierdie “doringagtige onkruide” wat vir medisinale en ander voedselvoordele gebruik word. Hoe goed van God om ons voordele te gee te midde van die vloek!

Dood

Dit is die een “D” waaroor die meeste van ons liewer nie wil praat nie. In werklikheid, wanneer ons ons eerste asem neem, is ons een asem nader aan die dood. Alhoewel alle plante, diere en mense eendag sal sterf, voel ons dit steeds ongemaklik om daaroor te praat. Dit is heel normaal dat ons ’n wil om te lewe het, en as ons dit nie het nie, moet ons hulp soek om uit te vind waarom.

Inderdaad het die dood geen ouderdom nie. In my leeftyd het ek gehelp om doodgeborene te begrawe, mense so oud as 96 jaar oud, en elke ouderdom daartussenin. Ons lees van die pragtige paradys wat herstel is, gesien deur die Apostel Johannes in Openbaring, soos hy die Hemel beskryf. Sommige van die dinge wat hy noem is geen siekte, geen hartseer, geen skeiding, geen trane, geen verdere lyding en geen dood nie. Op ’n manier is die lewe net ’n draoefening vir die ewigheid. Ons kan nie hier bly nie, net soos die baba in die baarmoeder nie kan besluit dat dit nie die werklike wêreld wil betree nie. Met al ons hartseerste en versoekings dra ons liggame uit en vergaan. Met al die geweld, sonde en goddeloosheid om ons, sou ons regtig vir altyd in hierdie toestand hier wou bly? Eerder keer ons terug na die grond waarvan ons gemaak is — as as tot as en stof tot stof — in afwagting van die finale opstanding. Was dit nie genadig van ons getroue God om die sondige mens te weerhou om van die boom van die lewe te eet in sy huidige sondige, sterflike toestand nie? Kan ons God se getrouheid sien en dankbaar wees vir die voorsiening van fisiese dood?

Te midde van die vloek wat aan Eva gegee is, word die eerste profesie van die Messias geopenbaar. “En Ek sal vyandskap stel tussen jou en die vrou, en tussen jou saad en haar saad; dit sal sy hoof verpletter, en jy sal sy hakskeen verpletter” (Genesis 3:15). Hy is die oorwinnaar van die dood! Lof aan God vir Sy Getrouheid.

Ontbinding en bederf

Ontbinding en bederf is nog ’n “D” van die vloek. ’n Neut val op die grond, en gou verskyn ’n spruit. In ’n paar jaar sal dit ’n klein saailing wees. Jare verby, en eekhorings versamel die eikels wat elke herfs op die grond val. Dan, as ’n magtige eikeboom, vang dit ’n virus, sterf dit, en in ’n paar jaar bring ’n windstorm dit ter aarde. Hier keer dit terug na die grond terwyl dit ontbind en vergaan. Sedert die vloek verrot en vergaan alles. Gegewe al die plante, diere en mense wat in die laaste 6 000 jaar gesterf het, is dit nie goed van God om ontbinding en bederf ontwerp te hê nie? Hoe sou hierdie wêreld gelyk het as al die rommel van 6 000 jaar nog oral geleë was? Die aarde sou bedek wees met dooie bome en lappe! Dit mag moeilik wees om te besef, maar God het hele koninkryke in die skepping ontwerp net om dit te bewerkstellig voordat dit selfs nodig was omdat Hy die behoefte voorsien het. Die koninkryke van gis, skimmel en fungus, die koninkryke van bakterieë, ensieme, en microskopiese plant- en dierelewe help almal om die vesel van die lewe af te breek en dit in die perfekte kunsmis te maak vir die voltooiing van die lewensiklus en voorsiening vir die volgende generasie. Gesonde organiese grond het ongeveer 8 miljard grondmikrobes in ’n enkele teelepel. Dit is nog ’n rede hoekom dit so belangrik is om die grond met respek te behandel, nie met harde chemikalieë nie.

Het jy al ooit oor die groot vloed van Noag gedink? Stel jou die miljoene ton plant-, dier- en menslike materiaal voor wat rondgedryf het voordat dit uiteindelik op die bodem neergesit en vinnig in sedimente begrawe is toe die waters terugtrek. Dit het die ideale toestande geskep om steenkool en ander fossielbrandstowwe wat ons vandag gebruik, te vorm. Daar was dit, diep binne die aarde, totdat die dag dit ontdek is. Tot vandag toe word dit nog gebruik.

Mag ons verantwoordelike en getroue rentmeesters van die Here se aarde wees!

“Want die gansche skepping verwag vol aandrang die openbaarwording van die kinders van God. Die skepping is onderworpe aan verganklikheid — nie uit eie wil nie, maar deur Hom wat dit onderworpe het, in die hoop — dat ook die skepping self sal verlos word uit die dienstbaarheid van verderwing tot die vryheid van die heerlikheid van die kinders van God. Want ons weet dat die ganse skepping tot dusver saam kreun en geboorte‑pyn ervaar. En nie alleen die ganse skepping nie, maar ook ons wat die eerstelinge van die Gees het, kreun binne ons en smag na die aanneming as kinders, dit is, die verlossing van ons liggaam” (Romans 8:19-23).

The winter of 1882 unfolded in the small southern town of Tuscumbia, Alabama. A happy, normal two-year-old girl fell desperately ill with a strange fever. The fever came and went, came and went, and came again. The family doctor feared the child would die of the strain, but the child was strong and one day the fever finally left for good. The following day the mother waved a hand past her daughter's face, but the child did not blink. Subsequent efforts wrought no results and a new day dawned upon the family with a blind daughter.

As the child gained strength enough to resume play, the great dinner bell released its peal to all around, but Helen did not respond. Other noises produced similar results and the Keller family came to the stark realization that life would never be the same again. Most of us may never face the grim circumstances that Helen Keller's family did, but each of us will certainly endure hardships tailored specifically by our God.

The human mind is an amazing and intricate creation. Though many have sought to understand it, its operational ability remains incomprehensible to mankind. It is no small wonder that a portion of the keenest insight into the health of the mind is revealed in God's Word. “For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.” (2 Timothy 1:7)

Fear is the ominous adversary to a sound mind. It towers over the soul and taunts the saint with its menacing derision. Fear can take a sunny meadow and turn it into a lonely wilderness. It can render a grand wedding celebration as dark as a cave, and turn a banquet fit for a king into a nauseating affair. It is the most powerful and devastating tool in the devil's employment. Despite many bold claims, none are exempt from its wielding. “A dreadful sound is in his ears: in prosperity the destroyer shall come upon him. He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, and he is waited for of the sword.” (Job 15:21, 22) It is fear that stands to attack and quench all the prosperity of the soul. If we are to resist it in these days, we he must rise with all diligence in defiant warfare.

We do not need to look very far to behold the disarmament and weakening of man's mind. Medication for the mind ranks among the leading prescriptions consumed in America today. This is no pointed accusation at any individuals who may find themselves in need of medical assistance to control their mind. But it takes no scholar to look at obesity and consider the diet, to see rebellious teens and connect it to the infrastructure of the home, or to see men's hearts (minds) failing them and believe that fear is at the root. While some may totally master their diet, few can claim to be accomplished parents. Fewer yet are those who are not, at times, accosted by fear. Though pride and sense may keep the outward man in check, and remaining perfectly calm, the inward man, at least subconsciously, must deal with the strain. Americans love to claim the motto, "No fear!" but our medication consumption tells a different story. Paul claimed no exemption, for he was “troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears.” (2 Corinthians 7:5)

What do we fear? Loss, pain, and humility. No one likes to lose something that we have fought to obtain. No one enjoys pain. No one loves to be humiliated. Still, we do not need to read far in the Scriptures to realize that these are often the avenues that God uses to further urge His servants down the path into His likeness. There is no insurance on earth that can secure the vibrancy of youth, the love of a family, or the respect of friends. The things that supply us with earth's greatest vanguard are all vulnerable to the risks of loss. Therefore, we fear. Though we lie in bed until the dawn of the morning, we can in no wise increase our stature nor alleviate the loss that God has laid upon our lives. This anxiety only furthers our grief and adds fuel to our fears.

“Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6 7) Herein is the keeping of our hearts and minds: prayer, peace, and thanksgiving.

Like a skillful artisan we must carefully weave these two scriptures together on the loom of life for there seems to be a direct correlation between the fruitful - power, love and sound mind, to the “rootful”- prayer, peace, and thankfulness. There will be no conquering of our fears without these things, and every society that is anemic to these ingredients will certainly be handicapped.

Prayer Begets Power

In our weakened condition we cannot apprehend prayer as we ought. It is then we must rely on those who can or perhaps the Spirit, which maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered. Communing with the Omnipotent Head of the universe is a tremendously bold task. Many will administer prayer as merely a formal task, seeking to be perfectly reverent in it. This is not communing as with a friend, nor is it bold. It is more apt to fall under the description of fear. The remedial therapy for fear is in pouring out all our anxiety, bitterness, and complaint onto our God. The saints of yesteryear had been known to vehemently pour out their accusations and the bitterness of their soul unto God.

“Then Job answered and said, Even to day is my complaint bitter: my stroke is heavier than my groaning. Oh that I knew where I might find him! That I might come even to his seat! I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me. Will he plead against me with his great power? No; but he would put strength in me.” (Job 23:1-6)

  • David —“I poured out my complaint before him; I shewed before him my trouble.” (Psalm 142:2)
  • Hannah —“For out of the abundance of my complaint and grief have I spoken hitherto.” (1 Samuel 1:16)
  • Jeremiah —“He hath filled me with bitterness, he hath made me drunken with wormwood.”
    (Lamentations 3:15)
  • Naomi —“Call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.” (Ruth 1:20)
  • Hezekiah —“He will cut me off with pining sickness: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me.” (Isaiah 38:12)
  • Jesus — “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46)

All these spewed forth bold accusations and complaints against God in fervent prayer and none of them offended Him. On the contrary, God had not given them the spirit of fear but of power, and they serve as our examples. It was faithless Ahab who was told to ask of God a sign in the heavens or earth. In his pious reply he refused to "tempt" God. This lack of boldness and abundance of fear is more tempting to God than the abundance of bitterness in our complaint for “there is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.” (1 John 4:18)

Peace Begets Love

We are all at rest with the things we love. "Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them.” (Psalm 119:165) A sparkling young child who is at peace with his father worships the man and strives to imitate him. Through the lad's tender eyes, his father's character is unflawed. His skill is unmatched. Even the brand of vehicle he drives is the best, and he emulates his every action. Even though every father knows the limitations of his son's expectations, we all bask in the seasonal loyalty. It is knowledge and fear that undermines this loyal love. An abusive father will destroy such childhood esteem and fear will be its replacement. It was through base fear that the evil servant buried his talent and did not trade with it. In his eyes his master was austere and to be feared. But God has not given us the spirit of fear but of love.

“We love him, because he first loved us. If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 John 4:19, 20) The soul who is affected by this love cannot but imitate it. He is at great peace with his Father’s love and the eyes through which he views his Father's character can only enlist replication. However dire the circumstances we may find ourselves in, this spirit of love and peace will carry us through whatever opposition we may meet with on life's pathway. Jacob made nothing of the hard service he was to endure for Rachel; the spirit of love to God will set us above the fear of man, and all the hurt that a man can do us.

Thankfulness Begets a Sound Mind

We do not need to study happy souls long to find buried within the bedrock of each one, a foundation of gratitude. The spirit of a sound mind, or quietness of mind, is a peaceable enjoyment of life. We are oftentimes discouraged in our way when the features of our environment do not measure not up to our own fancy and imagination. A mere sober, solid, thinking mind would obviate and defuse such fruitless notions, yet we are all tempted to entertain formidable ingratitude. It takes no brainpower to expose things we disdain, for Satan is certain to magnify and outline every unsatisfactory detail we encounter. We each may think ourselves into a deep cave, but we must thank ourselves out.

Fear of losing our health, wealth, reputation, and happiness is the biggest hindrance to securing it. To focus on our pain is to invite more. To be constantly analyzing our life to see if we are being fulfilled is a sure avenue to ingratitude. The world is constantly asking, "Are we having fun yet?" The answer is, "No". To these souls, life will never be adequate, and they must wander forth seeking the bigger fulfillment that the last one did not secure. It is the fear that we are not receiving our fair allotment in life that breeds discontentment. It is discontentment that produces more fear, and the downward spiral progresses. Such was the consternation of the soul who asked Christ to speak to his brother to divide the inheritance with him. This may be logical thinking, but it is not conducive to a sound and peaceable mind. This offended soul has no root in himself and will forever be wronged in some fashion and spend his days in search of a savior to come and fix the other party. “... neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.” (Isaiah 8:12, 13)

There is no earthly level of attainment or perfect environment that will promote a sound mind. It can only be secured through prayer, peace, and thankfulness. This may take some reprogramming of our minds to reach into the subconscious recesses, but we must soberly gird up the loins of our minds and exercise them if we ever hope to obtain “the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ;” (1 Peter 1:13)

Die winter van 1882 het ontvou in die klein suidelike dorpie Tuscumbia, Alabama. ’n Gelukkige, normale tweejarige meisietjie het wanhopig siek geword met ’n vreemde koors. Die koors het gekom en gegaan, gekom en gegaan, en toe weer gekom. Die familiearts was bevrees dat die kind sou sterf aan die spanning, maar die kind was sterk en op ’n dag het die koors uiteindelik vir ewig weggegaan. Die volgende dag het die moeder ’n hand by haar dogter se gesig verbygewaai, maar die kind het nie geknipper nie. Verdere pogings het geen uitslag gebring nie en ’n nuwe dag het vir die familie aangebreek met ’n blinde dogter.

Nadat die kind genoeg krag teruggekry het om weer te speel, het die groot aandete-klok sy geluid uitgestraal na almal rondom, maar Helen het nie gereageer nie. Ander geluide het soortgelyke resultate opgelewer en die Keller‑gesin het die skerp besef gekry dat die lewe nooit weer dieselfde sou wees nie. Die meeste van ons gaan moontlik nooit die grimmige omstandighede ervaar wat Helen Keller se familie moes deurmaak nie, maar elk van ons sal beslis swaarkry ondervind wat spesifiek deur ons God op ons pad geplaas word.

Die menslike verstand is ’n wonderlike en ingewikkelde skepping. Al het baie mense probeer om dit te verstaan, bly sy werksaamheid onbegrypelik vir die mensdom. Dit is geen geringe wonder dat ’n gedeelte van die skerpste insig in die gesondheid van die verstand in God se Woord geopenbaar word nie. “For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.” (2 Timothy 1:7)

Vrees is die dreigende vyand van ’n gesonde verstand. Dit torings oor die siel en terg die heilige met sy dreigende spot. Vrees kan ’n sonnige weiding omskep in ’n eensame wildernis. Dit kan ’n groot huweliksviering so donker maak soos ’n grot, en ’n feesmaal geskik vir ’n koning in ’n naarlike aangeleentheid omskep. Dit is die kragtigste en vernietigendste werktuig in die duiwel se diens. Ondanks baie stoutoplarings is niemand uitgezonder van sy beheer nie. “A dreadful sound is in his ears: in prosperity the destroyer shall come upon him. He believeth not that he shall return out of darkness, and he is waited for of the sword.” (Job 15:21, 22) Dit is vrees wat staan om aan te val en al die voorspoed van die siel te blus. As ons dit in hierdie dae wil weerstaan, moet ons met alle ywer in ’n uitdagende oorlog optree.

Ons hoef nie ver te soek om die ontwapening en verswakking van die mens se verstand te sien nie. Medikasie vir die verstand staan vandag onder die voorste voorskrifte wat in Amerika verbruik word. Dit is geen spitse beskuldiging teen enigiemand wat moontlik mediese hulp benodig om hul verstand te beheer nie. Maar dit verg geen geleerde nie om na vetsug te kyk en oorweeg dat dit met dieet verband hou, om rebelse tieners te sien en dit te koppel aan die huis se infrastruktuur, of om mans se harte (gedagtes) te sien faal en te glo dat vrees by die wortel lê. Terwyl sommige hul dieet heeltemal bemeester mag hê, kan min beweer dat hulle uitnemende ouers is. Nog minder is dié wat nie soms deur vrees aangeval word nie. Al hou trots en sin die uiterlike mens in die mou en bly hy uiterlik kalm, moet die innerlike mens, ten minste onderbewus, die spanning hanteer. Amerikaners hou daarvan om die motto te beweer, "No fear!" maar ons medikasieverbruik vertel ’n ander storie. Paulus het geen uitsondering geclaim nie, want hy was “troubled on every side; without were fightings, within were fears.” (2 Corinthians 7:5)

Waarvoor vrees ons? Verlore, pyn en vernedering. Niemand hou daarvan om iets te verloor waarvoor ons gestoei het om dit te verkry nie. Niemand geniet pyn nie. Niemand hou daarvan om verneder te word nie. Tog hoef ons nie ver in die Skrifte te lees om te besef dat dit dikwels die paaie is wat God gebruik om Sy dienaars verder aan te spoor op die pad na Sy gelykvormigheid nie. Daar is geen versekering op aarde wat die jeug se lewenskragtigheid, ’n familie se liefde of die vriendskap se respek kan waarborg nie. Die dinge wat ons van die aarde se grootste voorhoede voorsien, is almal vatbaar vir die risiko’s van verlies. Daarom vrees ons. Al lê ons in die bed tot die nuwe dagbreek, kan ons op geen wyse ons gestalte vermeerder of die verlies wat God op ons lewe geplaas het verlig nie. Hierdie kommer vergroot net ons hartseer en voeg brandstof by ons vrese.

“Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6 7) Hierin lê die bewaring van ons harte en gedagtes: gebed, vrede, en dankbaarheid.

Soos ’n bekwame ambagsman moet ons hierdie twee Skrifte versigtig saamweef op die leem van die lewe, want daar blyk ’n direkte korrelasie te wees tussen die vrugtbare - krag, liefde en ’n gesonde verstand, en die "wortelvolle" - gebed, vrede, en dankbaarheid. Daar sal geen oorwinning oor ons vrese wees sonder hierdie dinge nie, en elke samelewing wat arm is aan hierdie bestanddele sal beslis benadeel wees.

Gebed bewerk krag

In ons verswakte toestand kan ons nie gebed as wat dit behoort te wees begryp nie. Dan moet ons staatmaak op dié wat kan bid of miskien op die Gees, wat vir ons die innige gebede uitstort met onuitspreeklike gesmagte. Kommunikasie met die Almagtige Hoof van die heelal is ’n buitengewoon stoutmoedige taak. Baie sal gebed uitoefen as bloot ’n formele taak en poog om daarin volmaak eerbiedig te wees. Dit is nie gemeenskap met ’n vriend nie, en dit is nie stoutmoedig nie. Dit val meer geneig onder die beskrywing van vrees. Die remedie vir vrees lê in die uitgiet van al ons angs, bitterheid en gekla by ons God. Die heiliges van vroeër jare het bekend gestaan dat hulle hul aanklagte en die bitterheid van hul siel fel by God uitgegooi het.

“Then Job answered and said, Even to day is my complaint bitter: my stroke is heavier than my groaning. Oh that I knew where I might find him! That I might come even to his seat! I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me. Will he plead against me with his great power? No; but he would put strength in me.” (Job 23:1-6)

  • David —“I poured out my complaint before him; I shewed before him my trouble.” (Psalm 142:2)
  • Hannah —“For out of the abundance of my complaint and grief have I spoken hitherto.” (1 Samuel 1:16)
  • Jeremiah —“He hath filled me with bitterness, he hath made me drunken with wormwood.”
    (Lamentations 3:15)
  • Naomi —“Call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me.” (Ruth 1:20)
  • Hezekiah —“He will cut me off with pining sickness: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me.” (Isaiah 38:12)
  • Jesus — “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46)

Al hierdie het stoutmoedig aanklagte en klagtes teen God uitgespuit in vurige gebed en geen van hulle het Hom beledig nie. Inteendeel, God het hulle nie die gees van vrees gegee nie maar van krag, en hulle dien as ons voorbeelde. Dit was die ongelowige Ahab wat gesê is om ’n teken van God in die hemele of op die aarde te vra. In sy vroom reaksie het hy geweier om God te "beproef". Hierdie gebrek aan stoutmoedigheid en oorvloed van vrees is vir God meer versoeklik as die oorvloed van bitterheid in ons aanklag, want “there is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.” (1 John 4:18)

Vrede bewerk liefde

Ons is almal tevrede met die dinge wat ons liefhet. "Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them.” (Psalm 119:165) ’n Sprankelende jong kind wat in vrede met sy vader is, aanbid die man en poog om hom na te boots. Deur die jong se sagte oë is sy vader se karakter onbevlek. Sy vaardigheid is onvergelykbaar. Selfs die handelsmerk voertuig wat hy bestuur is die beste, en hy boots elke optrede van hom na. Al weet elke vader die beperkings van sy seun se verwagtinge, bad ons almal in die seisoenale lojaliteit. Dit is kennis en vrees wat hierdie lojale liefde ondermyn. ’n Mishandelende vader sal so ’n kinderagtige agting vernietig en vrees sal sy plek inneem. Dit was deur lae vrees dat die boosaardige dienskneg sy talente begrawe het en nie mee verhandel het nie. In sy oë was sy baas hartelik en om vrees te word. Maar God het ons nie die gees van vrees gegee nie maar van liefde.

“We love him, because he first loved us. If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” (1 John 4:19, 20) Die siel wat deur hierdie liefde aangeraak word, kan dit nie anders as om dit na te boots nie. Hy is in groot vrede met sy Vader se liefde en die oë waardeur hy sy Vader se karakter beskou, kan slegs nabootsing inroep. Hoe ellendig ook al die omstandighede mag wees waarin ons jouself bevind, hierdie gees van liefde en vrede sal ons deurdra tot watter teenstand ons ook al op lewenspaaie teëkom. Jakob het niks gemaak van die harde diens wat hy vir Rachel moes deurmaak nie; die gees van liefde tot God sal ons bo die vrees van die mens stel, en al die seer wat ’n mens ons kan aandoen.

Dankbaarheid bewerk ’n gesonde verstand

Ons hoef nie lank na gelukkige siele te bestudeer om te vind dat onder die fondasiebedding van elkeen ’n grondslag van dankbaarheid begrawe lê nie. Die gees van ’n gesonde verstand, of stilte van verstand, is ’n vreedsame genieting van die lewe. Ons word dikwels ontmoedig in ons pad wanneer die kenmerke van ons omgewing nie aan ons eie voorkeure en verbeelding voldoen nie. ’n Sober, stewige, nadenkende verstand sou sulke vrugtelose gedagtes voorkom en ontlont het, tog word ons almal versoek om formidabele ondankbaarheid te koester. Dit verg geen breinkrag nie om dinge bloot te lê wat ons verag, want Satan sal sekerlik elke ontevrede detail vergroot en uitlig wat ons teëkom. Ons elk kan onsself in ’n diep grot dink, maar ons moet onsself daaruit dank.

Vrees om ons gesondheid, rykdom, reputasie en geluk te verloor, is die grootste versperring vir dit te beveilig. Om op ons pyn te fokus is om meer uit te nooi. Om konstant ons lewe te analiseer om te sien of ons vervul word, is ’n seker pad na ondankbaarheid. Die wêreld vra voortdurend, "Are we having fun yet?" Die antwoord is, "No". Vir hierdie siele sal die lewe nooit voldoende wees nie, en hulle moet verder dwaal op soek na die groter vervulling wat die laaste een nie behaal het nie. Dit is die vrees dat ons nie ons regverdige aandeel in die lewe ontvang nie wat ontevredenheid bewerk. Dit is ontevredenheid wat meer vrees voortbring, en die neerwaartse spiraal vorder. Sulke was die vertwyfeling van die siel wat Christus gevra het om met sy broer te praat om die erfenis met hom te deel. Dit mag logiese denke wees, maar dit is nie bevorderlik vir ’n gesonde en vreedsame verstand nie. Hierdie gegriefde siel het geen wortel in homself nie en sal vir altyd op een of ander wyse benadeel word en sy dae deurbring op soek na ’n verlosser wat moet kom en die ander party regmaak. “... neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.” (Isaiah 8:12, 13)

Daar is geen aardse vlak van bereik of perfekte omgewing wat ’n gesonde verstand sal bevorder nie. Dit kan slegs deur gebed, vrede, en dankbaarheid beveilig word. Dit mag ’n mate van herprogrammering van ons gedagtes verg om in die onderbewuste gange te dring, maar ons moet soberlik die lewens van ons gedagtes omgord en dit oefen as ons ooit hoop om “the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ;” (1 Peter 1:13) te verkry.

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord –Luke 4:18-19.

Jesus was in His hometown of Nazareth. It was on the Sabbath, and He stood to read the scripture as He had in the past. This Sabbath He read from Isaiah 61. When He finished, He said, …This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears –Luke 4:21.

This marked the beginning of Jesus’ earthly ministry. In this first sermon He described the nature of His ministry. Notice the many references in this passage to healing: healing to the brokenhearted, deliverance to the captives, recovering of sight to the blind, and liberty to the bruised. Jesus came to provide a remedy for our brokenness. He came to repair the damage that sin has brought into humanity.

In this article we will look at the possibility for healing that is found in Jesus. Healing is a process that requires inner restoration with outside remediation. Physical healing begins at the cellular level and restores physical function. Spiritual healing begins at the heart level and restores us to fullness of life. Jesus said, …I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly – John 10:10.

As Jesus walked the dusty paths of Judea, He encountered many who needed physical healing. It was His ability to heal that drew many to seek Him out and to follow him. Many brought their friends and family to Him for healing. There is in all of us a desire for healing and wholeness. In the garden of Eden, mankind was created to be whole. When we are not whole, we seek every possible cure. So, crowds gathered around Jesus hoping for healing.

One day as Jesus was journeying through Jericho, a blind man, Bartimaeus, heard that He was approaching. Hope sprang up in his breast. He began to call out to Jesus, “Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me.” They tried to silence him, but he called the louder, “Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me.”

He cast his coat aside and blindly rushed into the street. Jesus said to him, “What wilt thou that I should do unto thee?” He said, “Lord, that I might receive my sight.” Jesus’ response to this simple faith was, “Go thy way; thy faith hath made thee whole.” Immediately, he received his sight, and followed Jesus. This is just one example of Jesus’ healing ministry. The examples are many. He healed lepers. He healed paralytics. He healed men and women of unclean spirits.

Does Jesus still heal in our day? I would like to answer that question by sharing my own journey of healing. I realize that not all are healed. Even in Jesus’ day, not all were healed. But I want to share my journey of healing to demonstrate the interconnectedness of the physical and the spiritual.

I was diagnosed with cancer in May of 2020. Hearing a doctor say, “You have millions of cancer cells in your body”, brought me face to face with my mortality like never before. Oh, I knew that someday I would die, but that was always somewhere in the far distant future. Now I needed to face the fact that I had a disease growing within me which had the potential to destroy my body.

Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord: And the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he have committed sins, they shall be forgiven him. Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much –James 5:14-16.

I have always been a strong advocate of anointing with oil. Just like we are taught in the book of James, I called for the elders of the church and asked them to anoint me with oil. In the biblical teaching of God healing through the anointing with oil there are a number of things that are expected of those seeking the healing. There is: call[ing] for the elders of the church, the prayer of faith, pray[ing] one for another, Confess[ing] your faults one to another, the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man… and the list goes on. So, one of the necessities to seek healing through the anointing with oil is the clearing of the heart of any known, unconfessed sin. Hence, I searched my heart and cleansed my heart of anything that would hinder God’s healing of my body.

Notice the close correlation in this passage between the physical and the spiritual. I found in my journey of healing that the one affects the other. Physical healing begins with spiritual healing. A few drops of oil have no therapeutic benefit. This anointing with oil is primarily a spiritual exercise. If we practice this ordinance as James offered it, we cleanse our hearts inwardly and then we ask God for physical healing.

This was my first step to healing, but a long journey lay ahead. We consulted with multiple doctors and eventually we chose a treatment protocol that included radiation and hormone therapy. This treatment weakened me physically and made me feel my humanity. It made me more dependent on God and others and less confident in my own abilities. Living with weakness caused me to draw my strength from my Heavenly Father Who is the source of strength. I relied heavily on the encouragement and support that my wife and family offered.

There are some lessons that can only be learned through human weakness. It was for this reason that Paul was given a thorn in the flesh. He sought the Lord three times for healing. God’s answer came back always the same, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my strength is made perfect in your weakness.” I can testify that that is true.

I had multiple radiation treatments in January of 2021. I had scheduled a series of meetings for the month of February thinking that my treatments would be over, and I would be back to normal. What I did not realize was the delayed effect of radiation. I breezed through the treatments, but in February I experienced a lot of digestive issues and a lot of physical weakness.

I was expected to deliver a series of four sermons on four consecutive evenings. We prayed and although I could not get through the day without napping God provided supernatural strength for those evening messages. I praise God that His strength was made perfect in my weakness.

My doctors have plied their trade. I am grateful for the professional medical care that I received. I have done what I could with herbs and supplements and God has been merciful. My last bloodwork came back “undetectable”. May God be praised!

I am sharing my experience to show the correlation between the physical and the spiritual. Physical illness in my experience had a sanctifying effect on my spirit and spiritual renewal conditioned my body for healing. I will be forever grateful for the professional care given by my doctors, but even they realize the limits of their profession. On my last visit to my Medical Oncologist, he said to me, “Now we are going to trust the Lord.” Thank God for God-fearing doctors!

There are several examples in scripture that demonstrate this correlation between physical and spiritual healing. In Mark 2 when they let the paralytic down through the roof into the presence of Jesus, He said to the paralytic, “Thy sins be forgiven thee.” Then He said, “Rise up and walk.” When He was challenged by the Pharisees for forgiving sins, He said to them, “Which is easier to say rise up and walk or thy sins be forgiven”, demonstrating that He had the power to do both. If we believe that Jesus has the power to forgive our sins, do we also believe that He has the power to heal our bodies? I do!

In John 5, Jesus healed a man who lay by the pool of Bethesda. He had this infirmity for thirty-eight years. Jesus came by and healed him. Later when He met him in the temple He said to him, “Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee.” Note the correlation between the physical and the spiritual.

Physical infirmity has a tremendous potential to open our hearts to spiritual realities if we allow it to. The Psalmist said: Before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word –Psalm 119:67. Jesus said: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord –Luke 4:18-19.

Take a fresh look at our proof text for this article and notice that Jesus is offering more than physical healing. He promises healing to the brokenhearted, deliverance to the captives, and liberty to the bruised. These promises are of emotional healing—healing for the hurt that we receive as a result of living in a broken, sin-cursed world.

I am sure that there are many people reading this article who have experienced trauma that I know nothing about. But I want to assure you that you can be healed. Do you believe that? Do you believe that the pain can go away? Do you believe that you can be delivered from fear, anxiety, anger, and bitterness?

We addressed the correlation between spiritual and physical healing. There is also a correlation between spiritual and emotional healing. If you are experiencing a broken heart, Jesus wants to heal your broken heart. If you are a captive—if you are bound to a past or to an addiction that prevents your freedom—Jesus will set you free. If you have been bruised Jesus will heal you.

My wife and I are appalled at the large number of people in our Anabaptist churches that are turning to psych drugs (mind medication) and secular counseling to find solutions for emotional disorders. The Bible addresses most emotional disorders:

Fear

  • There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear –1 John 4:18.
  • What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee –Psalm 56:3.
  • “Fear not” is found 63 times in the Bible

Anxiety

  • Be careful [anxious] for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God –Philippians 4:6.

Anger

  • Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice –Ephesians 4:31.

This is just a sampling of emotional disorders that we encounter in life, and I realize that behind these emotions there is often deep-seated trauma. Your trauma is not an astonishment to Jesus. He may not have experienced your exact trauma, but he has gone to the depth of your pain, and he has come through it in victory.

For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need –Hebrews 4:15-16.

The gospel provides a holistic remedy to man’s sin problem. Our Anabaptist heritage has emphasized the fact that faith in Jesus affects every area of our lives. This faith motivates us to follow Jesus in very practical ways in our daily lives. This results in a life of radical nonconformity to the world around us.

This radical discipleship should also affect our emotional responses to difficult people and circumstances. Or have we become so emotionally fragile that if life does not give us exactly what we want it upsets our emotional equilibrium? Or maybe the gospel that we preach has become a litany of words that appeases the mind but has no effect on our soul.

Let us therefore fear, lest, a promise being left us of entering into his rest, any of you should seem to come short of it. For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it –Hebrews 4:1-2. Is our faith in God so weak (remember that in the Biblical accounts of healing, it was their faith that enabled the healing) that we have more faith in medication or in a board-certified secular counselor than we have in God and His Word?

This is a discipleship series. Come with me to the mountain where Jesus is teaching. Yes, there is a large crowd, but follow me closely, we will try to get close enough to hear. I hear His voice—He is saying something about “salt of the earth” and “light of the world.” Here is an empty space—just room for two. Let’s sit on the grass and listen:

“Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.

And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also. And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain. Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.

Ye have heard that it hath been said, Thou shalt love thy neighbour, and hate thine enemy. But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.”

These are radical teachings. Radical in that they are so opposite from our natural inclinations, and yet, this is the way of peace. Most of our negative emotions such as anger, fear, and anxiety can be remedied by applying these teachings of Jesus to our situations. This may sound overly simplistic, but that is the nature of the gospel and millions of people have found life and freedom through faith in Christ.

Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits: Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases; Who redeemeth thy life from destruction; who crowneth thee with lovingkindness and tender mercies; Who satisfieth thy mouth with good things; so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle’s –Psalm 103:1-5.
